input: Closely related to the question of performance is the question of how long materials of this class can be expected to last in service, and here too the published picture is far from consistent. Two groups have reported lifetime values for the same material class that differ by a wide margin, and at first sight the results appear to contradict one another directly. A closer look at the test conditions, however, suggests that the two groups were not really measuring the same thing. The dry series also held the material at its working state for long stretches between regenerations, while the humid series returned it to regeneration before its uptake had settled, so the two series age the material on different clocks as well. The group reporting the longer lifetime cycled the material under a dry feed gas and regenerated it gently, under conditions that place relatively little stress on the structure. The group reporting the shorter lifetime, by contrast, used a humid feed and regenerated fully after every cycle, which is a considerably more demanding regime. There is also a difference in what each group chose to count as the end of life: one group recorded the number of cycles completed before the uptake had fallen by a noticeable margin, while the other reported the time on stream before the outlet purity could no longer be maintained. These are not interchangeable measures, and part of the apparent conflict dissolves once the definitions are placed side by side. target: The lifetime values reported for this material class conflict, and the conflict is again one of test conditions. The longer lifetime comes from tests under a dry feed with gentle regeneration. The shorter comes from a humid feed with full regeneration after every cycle. Water in the feed and heat in regeneration are the two stresses that age the material, and the two test series differ in both. The end of life is also defined differently. One series counts cycles to a stated loss of uptake; the other counts time on stream to a loss of outlet purity. A cycle count and a time on stream cannot be compared directly, and the numerical gap between the two reports is partly a gap between definitions. The conditions also differ in a further respect: the dry tests hold the material at its working state for long stretches between regenerations, while the humid tests return it to regeneration before its uptake has settled, so the two series age the material on different clocks as well as under different stresses. None of this makes either report wrong. Each is a correct lifetime for the duty it applied, and the reports conflict only when they are read as lifetimes for one and the same duty. For the benchmark material in humid service, the shorter lifetime is preferred. It was measured under the stress the service applies, and the longer figure, measured dry, would overstate the life the material can be expected to give on a wet feed. The preference rests on a stated condition: the regeneration in service is as severe as the regeneration in the humid tests. Under gentler regeneration the humid figure is pessimistic, and the life would fall between the two reported values, at a point neither test series measures.
